\chapter{Five Sizes of When}
\label{ch:anoche-y-todavia}
\hlchaptermodality{322}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say last night, the week, early, right away and still in Spanish, and say why an -o on the end of temprano never becomes an -a.}

Complete ES-C322-todavia: place a thing at anoche, count in semanas, arrive temprano, answer enseguida, and say todavia no.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[anoche]{anoche — a word with another word inside it}

\label{lesson:ES-C322-anoche}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{patience, please}, then \emph{a piece of advice}. (\emph{Paciencia, por favor}; \emph{un consejo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la noche — you can hear it inside this word.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-NO-che}, stress on the middle. The \emph{ch} is one sound, as in \emph{church}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{anoche} — \textquotedblleft{}last night.\textquotedblright{}

Say it slowly and the seam shows: \emph{a} plus \emph{noche}. Latin said \textbf{ad noctem}, \emph{toward night}. Two words, spoken together for centuries, until the \emph{d} fell out and nobody heard a join any more.

That \emph{noctem} is one of the easiest Latin words to spot in English. Something \textbf{nocturnal} happens at night. A \textbf{nocturne} is a night piece of music. An \textbf{equinox} is \emph{aequi-nox}, the day when night is equal to the light.

Here is the thing to hold on to. \emph{Anoche} has no other form. It does not become \emph{anocha} for a woman or \emph{anoches} for two nights. Words like \emph{contento} and \emph{ocupado} switch their last letter because they are describing somebody. \emph{Anoche} is not describing anybody — it is saying \emph{when} — so there is nothing for it to agree with, and it never moves.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words that place a thing in time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{anoche}
  \item \emph{anoche, en casa}
  \item \emph{un consejo — anoche}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin words are inside \emph{anoche}? (\emph{Ad} and \emph{noctem} — toward night.) Why does \emph{anoche} never change its ending? (It says when, not what somebody is like.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la semana]{la semana — a number wearing a different coat}

\label{lesson:ES-C322-semana}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a piece of advice}, then \emph{last night}. (\emph{Un consejo}; \emph{anoche}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez — one of these is hiding here.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{se-MA-na}, three even beats with the stress in the middle. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la semana} — \textquotedblleft{}the week.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{septimāna} meant \emph{the set of seven}, from \textbf{septem}, seven. A week is not named for anything it does. It is named for how many days are in it.

Spanish already shows you the seven: \emph{siete}. Put \emph{siete} and \emph{semana} side by side and you can watch the same Latin \emph{septem} go two ways — the \emph{p} holding on in one word and dropping out of the other.

English got the seven three times over. \textbf{September} was the seventh month back when the year began in March, and the name stayed on after the count moved. A \textbf{septet} is seven players. And English \textbf{seven} itself is the very same root coming down the Germanic road instead of the Latin one.

\emph{Semana} takes \emph{la}, and for more than one you add the ending you know: \emph{semanas}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A stretch of time you can count in, sitting next to a night you can point at.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la semana}
  \item \emph{dos semanas}
  \item \emph{anoche — esta semana}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What number is inside \emph{semana}? (Seven — \emph{septem}, \emph{siete}.) Why is \emph{September} not the ninth month by name? (The year once began in March.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[temprano]{temprano — an -o that stays put}

\label{lesson:ES-C322-temprano}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{last night}, then \emph{two weeks}. (\emph{Anoche}; \emph{dos semanas}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el tiempo — the same Latin word, differently worn.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tem-PRA-no}, stress on the middle. The \emph{pr} runs straight together. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{temprano} — \textquotedblleft{}early.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{tempus}, in its longer form \textbf{tempor-}, was \emph{time}. \textbf{Temporānus} meant \emph{in good time}, \emph{in season} — said of fruit that ripened when it should.

You already have that root once. \emph{El tiempo} is \emph{tempus} after the \emph{-por-} fell out and the \emph{e} broke into \emph{ie}. \emph{Temprano} is the same \emph{tempus} with the \emph{-por-} still there, squeezed down to \emph{-pr-}. One Latin word, two Spanish shapes, and you can hear the middle of it in only one of them.

English keeps it plainly: a \textbf{tempo} is a rate of time, something \textbf{temporary} lasts only a while, \textbf{temporal} means belonging to time, and a \textbf{contemporary} shares your time.

Now the ending, which is a trap worth walking into on purpose. \emph{Temprano} ends in \emph{-o}. You have seen \emph{-o} switch to \emph{-a}: \emph{contento} and \emph{contenta}, \emph{ocupado} and \emph{ocupada}. \textbf{This one does not switch.} A woman does not arrive \emph{temprana}. She arrives \emph{temprano}, because the word is not saying what she is like — it is saying when she got there. The \emph{-o}/\emph{-a} switch belongs to words that describe somebody. This word describes when a thing happened, and a \emph{when} is not a \emph{he} or a \emph{she}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Proof that an \emph{-o} on the end is not a promise.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{temprano}
  \item \emph{María come temprano}
  \item \emph{anoche — esta semana — temprano}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which everyday word shares \emph{tempus} with \emph{temprano}? (\emph{El tiempo}.) And does \emph{temprano} become \emph{temprana} for a woman? (No — it says when, not what she is like.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[enseguida]{enseguida — the next thing, and nothing between}

\label{lesson:ES-C322-enseguida}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{two weeks}, then \emph{early}. (\emph{Dos semanas}; \emph{temprano}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item conseguir — the same following is inside it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en-se-GUI-da}. The \emph{u} after \emph{g} is silent: it is there to keep the \emph{g} hard. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{enseguida} — \textquotedblleft{}right away.\textquotedblright{}

It is \emph{en} plus \emph{seguida}: \textbf{in what follows}. Not \emph{soon} — \emph{next}. Whatever comes after this comes with nothing in between, and that is why it means immediately.

Underneath is Latin \textbf{sequī}, \emph{to follow}, one of the great root verbs. You have it already in \emph{conseguir}, to get something by following after it, and in \emph{según}, which is \emph{secundum} — \emph{following along}.

English is thick with it. A \textbf{sequence} is one thing following another. A \textbf{sequel} follows a story. A \textbf{consequence} is what follows from a cause. To \textbf{pursue} is to follow forward. And \textbf{second} is \emph{secundus}, \emph{the following one} — the number two is named for coming after the one.

The spelling carries a silent passenger. In \emph{gui}, the \emph{u} makes no sound at all. Without it the \emph{g} would soften before that \emph{i}, and the word would not be \emph{seguida} any more.

Like \emph{anoche} and \emph{temprano}, \emph{enseguida} never changes.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The answer somebody gives you when they mean \emph{now}, not \emph{later}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{enseguida}
  \item \emph{enseguida, por favor}
  \item \emph{temprano — enseguida}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{en seguida} mean, piece by piece? (In what follows.) Why is the \emph{u} in \emph{seguida} written at all? (To keep the \emph{g} hard before the \emph{i}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[todavía]{todavía — all the road, and still going}

\label{lesson:ES-C322-todavia}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{early}, then \emph{right away}. (\emph{Temprano}; \emph{enseguida}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item todo — the first half of this word is yours already.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{to-da-VÍ-a}, four beats. The accent on the \emph{í} pulls the \emph{i} and the \emph{a} apart, so they are two beats and not one glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{todavía} — \textquotedblleft{}still,\textquotedblright{} and with \emph{no} in front of it, \textquotedblleft{}not yet.\textquotedblright{}

Break it where it wants to break: \emph{\textbf{toda vía}}. \emph{Toda} is the \emph{todo} you have, in its \emph{-a} shape. \emph{Vía} is Latin \textbf{via}, a road.

\textbf{All the road.} That was the whole sense once: the thing has gone the entire way and is going still. Old Spanish used it for \emph{always}, and it narrowed into \emph{still} — which is what \emph{always} becomes when you point it at one moment.

The \emph{via} is easy to find in English. You travel \textbf{via} somewhere. A \textbf{viaduct} carries a road. To \textbf{deviate} is to go off the road. \textbf{Trivial} comes from \emph{tri-via}, a place where three roads meet — the kind of gossip exchanged at a crossroads. And \textbf{obvious} is \emph{ob viam}, \emph{lying in the road}: what you cannot help meeting.

\emph{Todavía no} is the pair you will need most. \emph{No} comes first: \emph{todavía no}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five ways to place a thing in time: a night behind you, a stretch you can count, a position in the day, the very next moment, and a thing that has not stopped. Only one of the five ends in \emph{-o}, and even that one refuses to change.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{todavía}
  \item \emph{todavía no}
  \item \emph{temprano — enseguida — todavía}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two words inside \emph{todavía}? (\emph{Toda} and \emph{vía} — all the road.) What does \emph{obvious} mean, word for word? (Lying in the road.)
\end{tcolorbox}
